analysis.one_liner: Requires cost-benefit analysis of major federal rules, lets Congress veto them, and suspends some rule deadlines for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a committee or floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten how federal agencies write major regulations. Every rule expected to cost the economy $100 million or more a year would need a formal cost-benefit analysis and a scientific risk assessment, with peer review, and could not take effect until Congress had 45 days to review it and had the chance to vote it down. It also would have suspended many statutory and even court-ordered rule deadlines for two years while agencies adapted, and would have required public disclosure of White House communications about pending rules. Banking, securities, monetary policy, and campaign-finance and broadcast rules were written out of the analysis requirements entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries would gain time and flexibility: major health, safety, and environmental rules would be delayed, alternatives like market-based mechanisms would have to be considered, and existing rules would face scheduled reviews aimed at finding ones that can be amended or eliminated. The public would gain transparency, including disclosure of all written and oral communications between the White House budget office and outside parties about pending rules. Financial firms would gain by exemption: their rulemaking would be excluded from the analysis and congressional review requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries; financial firms by exemption

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to publish cost-benefit analyses for major rules, describing who benefits and who bears the costs, and consider alternatives including no government action and market-based mechanisms.

Health, safety, and environmental rules would require formal risk assessments based on the best available science, reviewed by independent peer-review panels that include industry, labor, consumer, and public-interest representatives.
All written communications between the Office of Management and Budget and outside parties about a rule under review, and records of oral communications, would have to be disclosed to the public.
Agencies would have to provide opportunities for meaningful public participation and place all communications about regulatory review in the public rulemaking record.

analysis.who_pays: People waiting for new or updated health, safety, and environmental protections would wait longer: deadlines in statutes and even court orders requiring agencies to issue rules would be suspended for up to two years. Workers, consumers, and communities exposed to risks would bear the cost of that delay, and because the analyses themselves would largely be shielded from judicial review, courts could not second-guess a flawed analysis.
analysis.who_pays_short: People awaiting health and safety protections

drawbacks.text: All statutory deadlines for covered rulemaking during the first two years, including deadlines imposed by federal courts, would be suspended until the analysis requirements were met or six months past the deadline, delaying new protections.

Judicial review would be sharply limited: a court could vacate a rule only if the required analysis was wholly omitted, and determinations by the OMB Director or the President could not be reviewed by any court.

Rules involving internal revenue laws, banking safety, credit unions, housing finance enterprises, monetary policy, the Federal Election Commission, and certain FCC actions would be excluded from the major-rule definition, so their costs and benefits would face no required analysis.
Agencies would have to schedule review of existing rules, prioritizing those that 'most likely can be amended or eliminated,' putting established protections on a path toward possible repeal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions are real and would have opened up a process that at the time operated largely behind closed doors. But the bill's core mechanics run the other way: a two-year freeze on rule deadlines, including court-ordered ones, broad carve-outs for the financial sector, and judicial review limits that make the new paperwork hard to enforce. The analysis requirements could improve some rules, but the design gives regulated parties time and flexibility while giving people waiting for protections delay. On balance the bill trades slower, more analyzed rulemaking for weaker accountability, and its exceptions are not justified on the face of the text.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the sponsor gave introductory remarks on several days that July, and the committee never reported it out, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Glenn of Ohio introduced the bill on June 29, 1995, with 19 cosponsors: 16 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day.
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the floor on five more days in July 1995, but no further action was taken.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill's last listed action is the July 21, 1995 remarks, and it died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People and communities relying on existing and upcoming health, safety, and environmental rules kept the current system, since the bill would have suspended rule deadlines for two years and put existing protections on a review track that could end in amendment or repeal. Agencies also avoided a new layer of analysis and reporting requirements. Regulated industries kept the status quo but lost the delays and flexibility the bill would have given them, and never got the chance to revisit rules under the ten-year review schedule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on existing health and safety rules

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 29, 1995 and never reported it out, held no recorded markup, and let it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Led the Senate's 1995 regulatory reform effort through a rival, more sweeping Republican bill, and S. 1001 was never brought to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship leaned Democratic — 16 of 47 Senate Democrats versus 3 of 53 Senate Republicans — and the Republican-run committee never advanced the bill.

industries.industry: Financial services, banking, and housing finance
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes rules on banking safety and soundness, credit unions, housing finance enterprises, monetary policy, and certain election and broadcast rules from the major-rule analysis and congressional review requirements. Financial regulators would have faced none of the new cost-benefit process their counterparts at EPA, OSHA, and FDA would bear.

industries.industry: Health, safety, and environmental regulated industries (chemicals, energy, manufacturing, mining, transportation)
industries.note: The bill would have delayed major rules for up to two years, required agencies to prioritize rules that can be amended or eliminated in scheduled reviews, and pushed agencies toward market-based mechanisms. Those gains come at the expense of people waiting for the underlying protections, though the added analysis and peer review could also produce better-documented rules.

Small entities would gain a new right to petition for judicial review of an agency's certification that a rule has no significant small-business impact, with courts able to order corrective analysis or stay rules.
